Chapter Four: Maintaining the Archive The internal wiki had been assembled over eleven years, first by hand, then by a handful of scripts that scraped old pages and stitched the fragments back together. The scripts were brittle. The guide warned about them at length, describing three separate migrations that had silently dropped entire sections of the archive, and it told readers to compare checksums before and after every batch job, keeping a copy of the raw output in case something went wrong. Nobody had ever been punished for skipping that step, the author conceded, but the one time it mattered the loss had taken a fortnight to repair. By the third section the tone had shifted from warning to instruction. The author explained that each page was stored twice, once as plain text and once as a fragment the renderer could splice into the surrounding layout. Naming conventions followed. Fragment files took the page title, lowercased, with spaces replaced by hyphens, and carried a two digit revision suffix. Anything imported from the old system kept its original name and was marked with a trailing underscore so that the migration scripts could find it later. Reviewers were asked to check the suffix before approving a merge, because a fragment with the wrong revision number would render but never appear in search results. The review process itself was described in tedious detail. Two reviewers were required for any change to a template, one for changes to prose. Comments had to be resolved before the request could be merged, and the automated checks had to pass twice, once on the branch and once after the rebase. The author admitted that the second check was mostly ceremonial, a relic of an earlier workflow, but argued that removing it would confuse the people who had learned the rules the hard way. A later appendix listed the exceptions, of which there were more than anyone expected. A chapter on the search index came next. Rebuilding it took forty minutes on a good day and considerably longer when the cache was cold. The guide suggested running the rebuild overnight and reminded readers that the job would fail quietly if the temporary directory filled up, which it did roughly once a quarter. Logs were rotated weekly and kept for ninety days, long enough, the author hoped, to explain any strange result that surfaced after the fact. The renderer itself was covered in a single paragraph. It read each fragment, wrapped it in the site template, and wrote the result to a cache keyed by the page title. When the template changed, every cached page had to be thrown away, and the guide suggested deleting the cache directory rather than trying to invalidate entries one at a time. The author noted that this advice had caused one outage, in the spring of the second year, and offered no apology for it. It was only in the final section, almost as an afterthought, that the guide showed what a finished fragment looked like in context:

Remember to rebuild the index after editing any fragment.

The example was followed by a short caution about caching, then by a list of contacts, most of them out of date, and a closing note on the difference between a redirect and a rename. A redirect preserved the old address and forwarded visitors to the new one; a rename broke every link that pointed at the old page. The distinction mattered mostly for external sites, which the team could not edit, and the note ended with a warning that the redirect table had never been audited. Nobody had updated the guide in three years. New contributors read the first two sections, skipped the rest, and asked their questions in the chat channel instead.
